CHAPTER XLIV

Experienced women are not frightened when a woman faints, or do they
hastily attribute it to anything but physical causes, which they have
often seen produce it. Catherine bustled about; laid the girl down with
her head on the floor quite flat, opened the window, and unloosed her
dress as she lay. Not till she had done all this did she step to the
door and say, rather loudly:

“Come here, if you please.”

Margaret Van Eyck and Reicht came, and found Margaret lying quite flat,
and Catherine beating her hands.

“Oh, my poor girl! What have you done to her?”

“Me?” said Catherine angrily.

“What has happened, then?”

“Nothing, madam; nothing more than is natural in her situation.”

Margaret Van Eyck coloured with ire.

“You do well to speak so coolly,” said she, “you that are the cause of
her situation.”

“That I am not,” said Catherine bluntly; “nor any woman born.”

“What! was it not you and your husband that kept them apart? and now he
has gone to Italy all alone. Situation indeed! You have broken her heart
amongst you.”

“Why, madam? Who is it then? in Heaven's name! To hear you, one would
think this was my Gerard's lass. But that can't be. This fur never cost
less than five crowns the ell; besides, this young gentlewoman is a
wife; or ought to be.”

“Of course she ought. And who is the cause she is none? Who came before
them at the very altar?”

“God forgive them, whoever it was,” said Catherine gravely; “me it was
not, nor my man.”

“Well,” said the other, a little softened, “now you have seen her,
perhaps you will not be quite so bitter against her madam. She is coming
to, thank Heaven.”

“Me bitter against her?” said Catherine; “no, that is all over. Poor
soul! trouble behind her and trouble afore her; and to think of my
setting her, of all living women, to read Gerard's letter to me. Ay, and
that was what made her go off, I'll be sworn. She is coming to. What,
sweetheart! be not afeard, none are here but friends.”

They seated her in an easy chair. As the colour was creeping back to her
face and lips. Catherine drew Margaret Van Eyck aside.

“Is she staying with you, if you please?”

“No, madam.”

“I wouldn't let her go back to Sevenbergen to-night, then.”

“That is as she pleases. She still refuses to bide the night.”

“Ay, but you are older than she is; you can make her. There, she is
beginning to notice.”

Catherine then put her mouth to Margaret Van Eyck's ear for half a
moment; it did not seem time enough to whisper a word, far less a
sentence. But on some topics females can flash communication to female
like lightning, or thought itself.

The old lady started, and whispered back--

“It's false! it is a calumny! it is monstrous! look at her face. It is
blasphemy to accuse such a face.”

“Tut! tut! tut!” said the other; “you might as well say this is not my
hand. I ought to know; and I tell ye it is so.”

Then, much to Margaret Van Eyck's surprise, she went up to the girl, and
taking her round the neck, kissed her warmly.

“I suffered for Gerard, and you shed your blood for him I do hear; his
own words show me that I have been to blame, the very words you have
read to me. Ay, Gerard, my child, I have held aloof from her; but I'll
make it up to her once I begin. You are my daughter from this hour.”

Another warm embrace sealed this hasty compact, and the woman of impulse
was gone.

Margaret lay back in her chair, and a feeble smile stole over her face.
Gerard's mother had kissed her and called her daughter; but the next
moment she saw her old friend looking at her with a vexed air.

“I wonder you let that woman kiss you.”

“His mother!” murmured Margaret, half reproachfully.

“Mother, or no mother, you would not let her touch you if you knew what
she whispered in my ear about you.”

“About me?” said Margaret faintly.

“Ay, about you, whom she never saw till to-night.” The old lady was
proceeding, with some hesitation and choice of language, to make
Margaret share her indignation, when an unlooked-for interruption closed
her lips.

The young woman slid from her chair to her knees, and began to pray
piteously to her for pardon. From the words and the manner of her
penitence a bystander would have gathered she had inflicted some cruel
wrong, some intolerable insult, upon her venerable friend.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER TWO.
[Reference Rewrite]: To comprehend the architecture of my early exile, one must first understand the absolute poverty of my universe at the age of seven. I existed within a microscopic empire of two, subjugated by a man I was conditioned to call "Master." He was a square-built, brutal artifact of a world I did not know, roughly sixty years of age, though time on the island seemed measured only by the decay of his humanity. His dark hair fell in matted, feral clusters, and a vast beard obscured his face, rendering him less a man than a beast draped in the ruin of whatever civilization had cast him out. He possessed a terrifying latent power, yet he spent his days in a state of stagnant lethargy, only stirring to exert his dominance over my labor—collecting sea-birds or hauling faggots of wood down the ravine.

Our lives were bound by the daily ritual of bathing in a salt-water pool, barricaded from the shark-infested ocean by a ridge of jagged stone. Beyond this, my existence was an enforced void. I was permitted no education, no heritage, and almost no language. The Master utilized silence as a tool of oppression, rationing his words to commands and curses, ensuring my mind remained as barren as the rocky crags that caged us. I became a taciturn creature, my intellect starved, left to gaze into the abyssal depths of the ocean or trace the cold geometries of the stars. I was kept as a beast of the field—valuable only for the calories my labor saved him, and perhaps to serve as a mirror for his own desperate need for mastery.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER THREE.

I left him, and commenced a careful descent of the precipices by which we were surrounded, but, before I had gone fifty paces, another flash of lightning was followed up by a loud shriek, which arrested my steps. Where the noise came from I could not tell, but I heard my companion calling to me to come back. I obeyed him, and found him standing where I had left him.

"You called me, master?"

"Yes, I did; take my hand and lead me to the cabin."

I obeyed him, wondering why he asked me so to do. He gained his bed-place, and threw himself down on it.

"Bring the kid full of water," said he--"quick!"

I brought it, and he bathed his head and face. After a time, he threw himself back upon the bed-place, and groaned heavily.

"O God! It's all over with me," said he at last. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What's the matter, master?" said I.
[Reference Rewrite]: I left him in the dark, initiating a careful descent down the rain-slicked precipices that formed the carceral walls of our world. Before I had traversed fifty paces, a sudden rupture of lightning tore the sky, pursued instantly by a shriek so guttural it arrested my breath. It was a sound stripped of all former sovereignty. I could not trace its origin through the howling wind, but then I heard the voice—his voice, diminished and frantic—commanding my return.

I obeyed, stepping back over the jagged stone, and found him frozen exactly where I had left him.

"You called me, master?" I asked, testing the word on my tongue.

"Yes, I did. Take my hand. Lead me to the cabin."

I guided him, marveling at the sudden frailty in his grip. The hand that had so often struck me down now clung to my shoulder with the desperate dependency of a drowning man. He found his bedding and collapsed onto it, a ruined monument of flesh.

"Bring the kid full of water," he gasped. "Quick!"

I brought the vessel. He plunged his face into it, bathing his head as if trying to wash away the fire of the heavens. Presently, he fell back against the damp wood, a heavy groan escaping his chest. "O God! It is all over with me," he whispered into the gloom. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What is the matter, master?" I asked.

He offered no answer, sinking instead into a rhythmic liturgy of curses and moans. When he finally fell still, I slipped out again into the dying tempest.

Experienced women possess a stoicism that renders them immune to panic when a sister falls; they do not hastily conjure specters of moral failing, but rather diagnose the immediate physical collapse with the clinical detachment honed by observation. Catherine moved with the brisk efficiency of one who knows the body's fragility better than its secrets. She lowered the girl until her head rested flat upon the floor, flung open the shutter to invite the raw air, and loosened the corset that constricted the victim's breath. Only after these mechanical acts of rescue were complete did she turn to the threshold and command, her voice ringing with authoritative clarity: "Come here, if you please."

Margaret Van Eyck and Reicht entered to find the scene stark: the girl prone and pale, Catherine thrashing her hands in a futile rhythm of distress. "Oh, my poor girl! What have you done to her?" cried the elder woman, her composure fracturing under the weight of maternal instinct.

"Me?" Catherine snapped, her anger rising like steam from a boiling kettle. "What has happened, then?"

"Nothing, madam; nothing more than is natural in her situation," Reicht replied, attempting to soothe the storm.

Margaret Van Eyck flushed with a heat that betrayed her ire. "You do well to speak so coolly," she retorted, her eyes narrowing, "you that are the architect of her situation."

"That I am not," Catherine declared bluntly, her stance rigid. "Nor is any woman born."

"Was it not you and your husband who kept them apart?" Margaret pressed, her voice trembling with suppressed accusation. "And now he has fled to Italy all alone. 'Situation' indeed! You have shattered her heart amongst you."

"Why, madam? Who is it then? In Heaven's name!" Catherine recoiled slightly, scandalized. "To hear you, one would think this was my Gerard's lass. But that cannot be. This fur never cost less than five crowns the ell; besides, this young gentlewoman is a wife—or ought to be."

"Of course she ought," Margaret insisted, her tone sharpening. "And who is the cause she is none? Who stood before them at the very altar?"

"God forgive them, whoever it was," Catherine said gravely, shaking her head. "Me it was not, nor my man."

"Well," the other woman conceded, her anger softening into concern as she observed the girl's breathing deepen, "now you have seen her, perhaps you will not be quite so bitter against her, madam. She is coming to, thank Heaven."

"Bitter against her?" Catherine laughed, a dry, incredulous sound. "No, that is all over. Poor soul! Trouble behind her and trouble ahead; and to think of my setting her, of all living women, to read Gerard's letter to me. Ay, and that was what made her go off, I'll be sworn. She is coming to. What, sweetheart! Be not afraid, none are here but friends."

They lifted the girl into an easy chair. As color began to creep back to her cheeks and lips, Catherine drew Margaret Van Eyck aside, lowering her voice to a conspiratorial whisper. "Is she staying with you, if you please?"

"No, madam."

"I wouldn't let her go back to Sevenbergen tonight, then."

"That is as she pleases. She still refuses to bide the night."

"Ay, but you are older than she is; you can make her. There, she is beginning to notice."

Catherine leaned forward, pressing her mouth to Margaret Van Eyck's ear for a fleeting instant. It seemed insufficient time to whisper a word, far less a sentence, yet between women, communication flashes across the chasm of silence like lightning or pure thought itself. The old lady stiffened, her eyes widening in horror, and whispered back urgently.

"It is false! It is a calumny! It is monstrous! Look at her face. It is blasphemy to accuse such a face."

"Tut! Tut! Tut!" Margaret dismissed the warning with a wave of her hand. "You might as well say this is not my hand. I ought to know; and I tell you it is so."

Then, to Margaret Van Eyck's profound astonishment, she rose and took the girl by the neck, kissing her warmly, a gesture of fierce affection. "I suffered for Gerard, and you shed your blood for him, I do hear; his own words show me that I have been to blame, the very words you have read to me. Ay, Gerard, my child, I have held aloof from her; but I'll make it up to her once I begin. You are my daughter from this hour."

Another warm embrace sealed this hasty compact, and the woman of impulse vanished into the room. Margaret lay back in her chair, a feeble smile stealing over her face. Gerard's mother had kissed her and claimed her as kin; but the next moment, she saw her old friend regarding her with a vexed, troubled air.

"I wonder you let that woman kiss you," Margaret murmured, half-reproachful.

"Mother, or no mother, you would not let her touch you if you knew what she whispered in my ear about you," Margaret continued, her voice low.

"About me?" Margaret asked faintly.
